scenes.headline: How a staged harness rebuilds a photo in Blender
scenes.sub: SEIG's four stages, and which of its parts a stronger model eats.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Mambo! A research harness turns one photo into an editable Blender program. Here's how, and which parts a stronger model eats.

scenes.text: SEIG rebuilds a scene the way an artist works: geometry, then material, then composition, then lighting, each stage closed by its own verifier.
scenes.mark: geometry, then material, then composition, then lighting
scenes.say: Rebuild the scene the way an artist works: geometry, material, composition, then lighting, each closed by its own verifier.

scenes.title: From one photo to a Blender program

steps.say: From one photo, the model sketches four rough scenes. Every object gets a stable Blender name.
A selector keeps the one with the most complete coverage.
Then the four stages, each with a round budget: five for geometry, three each for material and composition, two for lighting.

steps.note: every intermediate is a coherent, editable scene
steps.say: Each stage commits before the next begins, so every step is an editable Blender program.

items.text: Generator edits through a scoped tool
items.say: Inside a stage, the generator edits through a tool scoped to it. The material tool can only make material edits.
Blender renders the result, and the verifier returns a checklist rather than a free critique.

items.text: Commit; no later stage undoes it
items.say: Once approved, the stage commits. No later stage may undo it.

scenes.label: PSNR the staging adds over an unstaged agent loop, on NeRF synthetic
scenes.note: one backbone, Claude Opus 4.7; the revisit reports no number
scenes.say: Staging was measured on one model: plus one point two five decibels. The revisit says the gain nearly vanishes on stronger models, with no number.

scenes.title: What each part stands in for

items.say: A substitute covers something the model can't do yet, like the staging itself. Scaling eats it.
Supply brings in a fact from outside, like the render.
A constraint forbids an outcome, like the material-only tool. It isn't eaten, but what it gives up grows more valuable.

scenes.text: Substitutes get eaten. Constraints get repriced: what a ban gives up is worth more as the model improves.

recap: Four stages, each a generator-verifier loop
scenes.say: To recap: four committed stages, and three kinds of scaffolding.
